To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

population structure and crypticism can be treated as the same confounding problem, that kinship coefficients can be used to quantify and adjust for confounding, and that mixed models can be used to analyze the data.

population structure and crypticism are two different aspects of the unobserved pedigrees of the study subjects, that the kinship coefficient is the central concept in the analysis of population structure, that linear mixed model analysis provides a powerful solution to the problem, and that recent advances in the theory of linear mixed models are enabling its widespread application in genetic association studies.

the problem of population stratification and cryptic related kinship can be viewed as a single confounder, that kinship is the central concept in the unified analysis, and that linear mixed models are an effective and computationally tractable solution to the problem.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the analysis of complex data from genetic association studies, and the use of statistical methods to detect the presence of population structure and relatedness, and to correct for its effects.
the development, implementation and evaluation of methods for the analysis of genetic data in the presence of population structure and relatedness.
the analysis of human genetic data, in particular, the development of methods to identify genetic factors influencing common diseases.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the problem of population stratification is a serious problem that must be taken into consideration in all studies, and there is no simple, single solution that can be recommended for all studies.
the best way to avoid the problem of confounders due to population structure and crypticism is to avoid the problem altogether by studying families.
the problem of confounded genetic association studies is not solved, but that there are a number of methods available to help deal with the problem.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the kinship coefficients of the study subjects are a confounder that can be estimated from the marker data, and that this can be used to protect against population structure, cryptic kinship and other forms of confounding.
we are now in a position to analyse human association data with confidence that we are not being fooled by population structure or cryptic relatedness.
the most important thing is to understand the population structure and kinship of the study subjects.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the problem of confounders in human genetic association studies should not be considered separately as population structure and cryptically related individuals.
the pedigree is a powerful tool for understanding the problem of confounders, and for developing solutions.
, when the pedigree is unobserved, the most effective way to deal with the confounder is to model it directly, using the observed marker data.
